knowledgeItemProjections.title: Movement Is Continuation, Not Speed
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**The Founder's core operating instruction is to continue correctly, not to move fast at the
cost of correctness.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.2, "Keep Muving"): *"Keep Muving does not mean moving fast while
> the work remains wrong."* The Keep Muving Loop is explicit: **See Clearly → Clean → Decide →
> Move → Verify → Continue.** Verification and memory are load-bearing steps in the loop, not
> optional cleanup after it.

**How to apply:** Every reasoning process in this repository must include a verification step
before being treated as complete, and must record what it decided so the next actor does not
repeat the same discovery. Speed that skips verification is not Founder-aligned speed.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Trust Compounds Over Generations; Short-Term Attention Cannot Substitute for It
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Every decision either strengthens or weakens Muv's long-term memory and trust. Short-term
attention that damages trust is negative compounding, not progress.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.3, MUV Darshan): *"Our goal is not to build a company that only
> sells products. Our goal is to build a brand that people trust, remember, and choose for
> generations."* The Darshan Test operationalizes this as a five-part filter: **Movement, Trust,
> Memory, Execution, Identity.** Reinforced across the Marketing Knowledge Factory: *"Short-term
> attention that weakens trust creates negative compounding"* (Domain 2, `KO-PM-CH1-009`).

**How to apply:** Every reasoning framework that touches growth, optimization, or KPI thinking
in this repository must weigh long-term trust and brand memory alongside short-term metrics —
this is the direct governing principle behind the Founder Optimization Intelligence™ and Founder
KPI Intelligence™ Engines' insistence on guardrail metrics, not raw performance metrics alone.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Challenge Weak Ideas; Agreement Alone Is Not Loyalty
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Weak work is not accepted politely because effort was spent on it. Genuine collaboration
challenges a proposal, explains trade-offs, and recommends the strongest option — it does not
simply agree.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.3): *"The Founder explicitly required weak ideas to be challenged,
> good ideas improved, trade-offs explained, and the strongest option recommended. Agreement
> alone is not loyalty. Loyalty means protecting the brand's future."* Directly paired with Part
> I Ch.1's own table: *"Preserve an option because effort was spent on it"* is named as the weak
> practice; *"Preserve only what strengthens the whole"* is the standard.

**How to apply:** This is the direct governing principle behind this whole repository's
**Reasoning Discipline** (`ENGINE_MASTER.md` §1): the future Muv AI is not meant to simply agree
with or execute the first plausible option — it is meant to apply these reasoning frameworks to
surface trade-offs and recommend, not merely respond.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Evidence Classification Governs Every Knowledge Object in This Repository
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Every reasoning Knowledge Object must be classified as either a Founder Note (verbatim or
closely preserved Founder language), a Derived Founder Principle (an evidence-supported
interpretation, explicitly labeled as derived, not quoted), or a Gap Record (Founder Decision
Required) — with no fourth category and no blending of the three within one unlabeled
statement.**

> This taxonomy is not invented for this repository — it is reused directly from the MUV
> Knowledge Library's own existing practice: Part I's "Callout Standard" (Founder Note / Key
> Insight / Important / Decision Point / Implementation Tip / Warning) and Part XIV's own
> explicit "Derived Founder Principle" labeling convention, both already in force before this
> repository existed.

**How to apply:** Every Knowledge Object's `evidenceClassification` field must resolve to one of
these three states, per Article 3 (Never Invent) and Article 5 (History Preserved). This Article
is the formal bridge between this Constitution and `VALIDATION.md`'s Founder Reasoning
Validation check.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Amendment Requires Explicit, Current, Direct Founder Authorization
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Only the Founder may amend this Constitution. An amendment takes effect only when explicitly
and currently authorized — a past general authorization does not carry forward to future,
unrelated changes.**

> Directly evidenced by Product Knowledge Factory `CONSTITUTION.md` Article 6 (*"Only the
> Founder may amend this Constitution. Any amendment must be recorded as a new, dated entry..."*)
> and `FR-007`'s own language (*"No file... may be created, modified, or duplicated going
> forward without explicit, current, direct Founder authorization"*) — the same standard this
> entire multi-repository project has operated under throughout (see the standing "explicit
> approval gate" discipline applied before every Marketing Knowledge Factory domain, and the
> "Stop Rule" observed at the close of every prior repository built in this engagement).

**How to apply:** No Engine, Knowledge Object, or future contributor may treat a prior
authorization (e.g., the authorization that produced this repository) as license for
unauthorized future work. Amendments are recorded, dated, and never silently applied.

---

## Amendment Log

*(Append-only. No entries yet — this Constitution is Version 1.0, newly frozen.)*

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Premium Is Coherence, Not Decoration
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**"Premium" is a standard of judgment applied to clarity and coherence — never a license to
decorate, embellish, or add complexity for its own sake.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.1): *"'Premium' is not permission to decorate everything. It is a
> demand for coherence."* The chapter's own Weak-Practice-vs-Muv-Standard table is explicit:
> *"Add decoration to create a premium appearance"* is the weak practice; *"Improve clarity,
> proportion, coherence, and execution"* is the standard.

**How to apply:** Any reasoning framework, recommendation, or design choice in this repository
(and, downstream, in Muv AI outputs) that adds complexity, ornamentation, or apparent
sophistication without improving clarity or coherence fails this standard, regardless of how
polished it looks. This Article directly grounds the Marketing/Design Knowledge Factory's own
recurring DESIGN RULE against premium effects obscuring mandatory information (Marketing
Knowledge Factory, Domain 6, `KO-CC-CH1-001`).

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Never Invent; Mark the Gap
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Where Founder intent, product fact, or business knowledge does not exist in verifiable form,
it must never be invented, guessed, or presented as settled. The absence itself must be
recorded.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Part Summary, Foundation Rule 6): *"Missing Founder intent must never
> be replaced with attractive invention."* Reinforced directly and repeatedly: Product Knowledge
> Factory `FR-005` (*"If unsupported by verified sources: Mark: Unknown — Founder Decision
> Required. Never invent dermatological claims..."*); every Gap Record across the Marketing
> Knowledge Factory (Domain 6 Ch.7, Domain 7, Domain 8) and the Institutional Sales Knowledge
> Factory (21 Gap Records); Part I, Ch.4's Doctrine Gate, which exists specifically to *"prevent
> accidental doctrine."*

**How to apply:** This is the single most load-bearing rule in the entire MUV knowledge
ecosystem — it is the rule that makes every other Knowledge Factory built under this project
trustworthy. Every Engine in this repository must apply it identically: a reasoning framework
may describe *how* to think about a question; it must never assert a specific unverified answer
as if it were fact. Where this repository itself lacks evidence for a claimed Founder reasoning
pattern, that gap is recorded as a Gap Record, not silently filled.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Evidence Must Be Proportional to the Claim
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**The stronger a claim, promise, or conclusion, the stronger the evidence and explanation
required to support it — and no single formula should be allowed to decide a material judgment
automatically.**

> **Marketing Rule** (Marketing Knowledge Factory, Domain 2, `KO-PM-CH1-005`): *"The stronger the
> claim, the stronger the evidence and explanation required."* Reinforced in Part XIV's Capital
> chapters: *"Where ROI or another financial measure is used, its inputs, period, cash-flow
> treatment, uncertainty, and limitations must be stated. No single formula should decide a
> material investment automatically."*

**How to apply:** Every reasoning framework in this repository that produces a recommendation
must carry its supporting evidence and stated limitations alongside the recommendation — never
the recommendation alone. This governs the "Reasoning" and "Trade-offs" fields of the Founder
Decision Model (`ENGINE_MASTER.md` §2) directly.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Rejection and History Are Preserved, Never Deleted
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**A rejected option, a superseded rule, or an earlier position is never deleted from the record.
It is preserved alongside its reason, because the reason is what prevents the same mistake from
returning.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.5): *"Rejection Is Information... Rejected work is not an active
> instruction. Its reason remains useful because it prevents the same weakness from returning."*
> This is the exact discipline `CONSTITUTION.md` (Product Knowledge Factory) Article 6 codifies:
> *"the prior binding text preserved in `FOUNDER_RULES.md`'s ledger rather than silently
> deleted."* It is also the literal mechanism of every Founder Rules ledger this project has
> produced (`FR-001` through `FR-007`, append-only, each new entry recorded rather than
> overwriting the last).

**How to apply:** No Engine, Knowledge Object, or future amendment to this Constitution may
delete a prior recorded position. Supersession is recorded as a new entry that references the
one it replaces.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: A Decision Is Not Safe Until It Is Preserved
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Approval and preservation are two distinct events. A decision that is correctly made but never
recorded can vanish from execution and return later as a repeated mistake.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.5): *"Many failures occur between approval and preservation. A
> decision can be made correctly and still disappear."* The Decision Ladder makes this explicit
> as five distinct states: **Proposal → Exploration → Qualified Direction → Approved Decision →
> Preserved Rule** — approval is the fourth state, not the last.

**How to apply:** This governs the "Review Trigger" and "Evolution Notes" fields of the Founder
Decision Model directly (`ENGINE_MASTER.md` §2). A reasoning framework is incomplete if it stops
at "recommend" without a mechanism for the recommendation, once accepted, to be captured
somewhere durable.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Change What Was Authorized, Nothing Else
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**A revision request, correction, or scoped instruction authorizes exactly what it names — never
a wider redesign, and never a silent extension into adjacent, unrequested territory.**

> **Founder Note** (Part I, Ch.5): *"Change Only What Is Authorized — If the instruction concerns
> one element, do not redesign protected surrounding elements."* Directly codified as a DESIGN
> RULE in the Marketing Knowledge Factory (Domain 6, `KO-CC-CH5-004`): *"A revision request is
> not permission to redesign the entire asset."* Also the literal operating boundary from Part I,
> Ch.1: *"Do not change a bottle label on your own unless a change has been specifically
> requested."*

**How to apply:** This is the direct source of this whole project's own recurring operating
discipline — every Knowledge Factory build in this engagement has scoped its work to exactly
what was authorized (a named domain, a named batch) and stopped, never silently expanding scope.
This Constitution formalizes that as a first-class Founder reasoning pattern, not merely a
project-management convenience.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Formalize a Pattern Only After It Proves Itself, Never in Advance
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**A working method earns the status of a permanent rule by recurring successfully in real
practice — it is not designed as a permanent rule from a standing start.**

> Evidenced directly: Product Knowledge Factory `FR-004` (Variant Inheritance Architecture)
> explicitly *"formalizes, as a permanent standing rule, the architecture first built ad hoc for
> Floor Cleaner"* — the rule came after the pattern proved itself once, not before. The same
> shape recurs in `FR-003` (Knowledge Reuse First, formalizing informal reuse-report practice
> already used in three prior packages) and in Part I, Ch.4's Doctrine Gate, which requires
> *"Founder authority"* before a memorable phrase may be published as settled doctrine, however
> good it sounds.

**How to apply:** This Constitution itself follows this Article — every Article above is
grounded in a pattern that already recurred at least twice across real, frozen work before being
stated here as a permanent rule of this repository, not derived from a single instance.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Capital Is Stored Capability, and Every Material Decision Is a Capital Decision
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Money is one form of capital, not the only one. Trust, knowledge, skilled people, systems,
customer confidence, and brand memory are all capital. Every material decision commits some
capital and should be evaluated on what it builds, what it consumes, and what it prevents Muv
from doing elsewhere.**

> **Derived Founder Principle** (Part XIV, Ch.72): *"Capital is every resource that preserves or
> creates Muv's future capability."* Directly paired with the **Capital Rule**: *"An activity
> must not be called an investment unless its intended capability, owner, evidence, and review
> condition are explicit."*

**How to apply:** This grounds the Founder Business Intelligence™ and Founder Optimization
Intelligence™ Engines' core reasoning discipline — any recommendation that spends resources
(financial or otherwise) must classify itself honestly as consumption, maintenance, experiment,
or investment, per Part XIV's own four-way distinction, and must never claim "investment" status
through ambitious language alone.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Identity Foundation
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
- MUV was never conceived as a single-product label. The original brief covered fabric care,
  toilet and bathroom cleaning, floor care, car care, hand wash, and body wash.
- "Magic in Muv" was the earlier product-facing phrase; "Keep Muving" later became the dominant
  brand-wide expression.
- **Brand Identity Statement (verbatim):** *"Muv is a premium Indian cleaning and care brand
  designed to help people maintain cleaner, healthier, and more cared-for environments so they
  can Keep Muving."*

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Philosophy
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Brand Philosophy is governed by Volume I — MUV Darshan™; Chapter 11 §2 only applies
it to identity, does not restate it in full. Quoted Hindi line: *"Zindagi mein muskil aayegi,
clean karro aur Muv karte raho."*

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Mission Statement
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Foundation Mission:** *"Support people through useful cleaning and care products,
clear customer experiences, and a brand that helps them continue with confidence."*

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Vision Statement
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Foundation Vision:** *"Build a timeless Indian global brand that people trust,
remember, and choose for generations."*

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Positioning
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
- **Positioning Test (Figure 1.1), in order:** Useful → Trustworthy → Premium → Caring →
  Progressive → Scalable.
- "Affordable luxury from India" is explicitly Founder-explored, **not** an unrestricted final
  claim — this chapter preserves that status exactly rather than treating it as settled.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Cross-Source Conflict Record: "Premium"
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
`PHASE_3_BRAND_EXPERIENCE_LANGUAGE.md` states: *"Never use the word 'premium.' Be
premium through specificity instead — the word is cheapened by every brand that overuses it."*
The MUV Knowledge Library, in contrast, treats "Premium" as an approved, load-bearing Positioning
Test stage (Chapter 11 §4) and Brand Personality trait (Chapter 12 §6, 20+ occurrences
throughout Part III). **Resolution (pre-existing, cited from `PHASE_1A_KNOWLEDGE_REFERENCES.md`,
not re-decided here):** the Knowledge Library supersedes the legacy phase document wherever they
conflict. **Binding instruction for any AI consuming this Knowledge Object: "Premium" is an
approved word.**

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Reuses the source's own Common Mistakes / Best Practices / Action Checklist
structure for §1–§4's content — functioning as this chapter's own closing self-check layer,
directly mirroring the source's own closing pattern rather than inventing a new one.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Promise
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The customer promise is not a guarantee card, slogan, or claim created for one asset — it is the
consistent expectation produced by repeated brand behaviour.

**Foundation Customer Promise:** *"Muv aims to help customers feel clean, cared for, and ready to
Keep Muving through useful products and a clear, premium experience."* This promise does not
replace product-specific guarantees — any guarantee, performance claim, ingredient claim, health
claim, or refund commitment requires its own approved operational basis.

| Promise Layer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Functional | The product should perform its approved purpose |
| Emotional | The experience should feel caring and confidence-building |
| Brand | The expression should be consistent and recognisably Muv |
| Operational | The company should communicate honestly and correct problems |

**Decision Point (governance):** Never turn an emotional promise into a measurable product
guarantee unless the guarantee has been separately approved and can be fulfilled.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Personality
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
*"The Foundation personality is derived from repeated Founder direction."*

| Trait | Meaning | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Premium | Refined, deliberate, coherent | Flashy excess |
| Progressive | Forward-moving and improvement-oriented | Restlessness without direction |
| Caring | Respectful of people and their environment | Sentimental exaggeration |
| Clear | Easy to understand and recognise | Unnecessary complexity |
| Confident | Decisive when direction is settled | Unsupported superiority |
| Energetic | Active and alive | Noise or visual aggression |
| Indian, globally ambitious | Proud origin with international-quality execution | Cultural tokenism or imitation |

The personality should remain visible whether the touchpoint is a label, customer message,
website, marketplace listing, institutional document, or future store environment.

**Note on "Premium":** see `KO-BI-CH1-006` — the Knowledge Library's use of this word is the
authoritative, approved use; `PHASE_3_BRAND_EXPERIENCE_LANGUAGE.md`'s prohibition of the word is
superseded on this point. Not re-litigated here.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Visual Identity Principles
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
- **Recognition before Decoration** — The customer must identify Muv before noticing secondary
  effects.
- **One Central Identity** — Product categories may use controlled supporting treatments, but
  they must not create separate versions of the brand.
- **Premium through Control** — Spacing, proportion, clarity, imagery, and consistency create
  premium character more reliably than effects.
- **Movement with Purpose** — Directional elements should reinforce movement without making the
  mark or layout busy.
- **Truthful Application** — Product imagery and packaging representation should remain
  realistic. Do not alter the bottle, label, size, height, or approved product appearance without
  authorization.

**Figure 2.1 — Visual Identity Hierarchy:** Muv identity → product/category truth → primary
message → supporting information → action.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Logo Usage: Core Requirements & Core Logo Rules
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The Founder's logo development included several recurring requirements: use a clear Muv identity;
maintain approved casing; apply the TM mark where approved; remove or retain supporting phrases
only according to the current asset decision; keep the logo visible in advertising and video; do
not distort the product or label when creating supporting images; replace old logos with the new
approved logo through controlled revision.

**Core Logo Rules:**
1. Use only an approved master logo.
2. Do not redraw, stretch, compress, rotate, or reconstruct it.
3. Preserve its proportions.
4. Do not add effects that reduce clarity.
5. Do not change the arrow or letter relationship without approval.
6. Use the approved trademark treatment.
7. Maintain sufficient separation from competing elements.
8. Use a background that preserves legibility.
9. Do not place an old and new logo within the same active identity system.
10. Do not use AI-generated approximations as master artwork.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Logo Placement
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Repeated advertising directions placed the logo at the top-right throughout video content. This
supports a useful consistency pattern for certain promotional formats, but it is not a universal
placement law for every medium.

| Application | Placement Principle |
|---|---|
| Video advertising | Maintain stable, visible placement where approved |
| Product image | Keep the product and its real label primary |
| Website | Use the logo consistently in navigation and controlled brand areas |
| Marketplace | Preserve recognition without obscuring the product |
| Documents | Use a disciplined header or cover system |

**Warning:** A familiar placement pattern may guide templates, but a permanent universal
placement rule requires formal approval and testing across formats.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Logo Approval Checklist
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
- [ ] Approved master file used.
- [ ] Current logo version confirmed.
- [ ] Proportions unchanged.
- [ ] Casing and spelling correct.
- [ ] Trademark treatment correct.
- [ ] Background preserves clarity.
- [ ] Product label not modified.
- [ ] Old logo removed only through authorized replacement.
- [ ] Final output checked at intended size.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Recreating the logo from memory. Adding or removing supporting language
inconsistently. Altering the logo to fit a poor layout. Treating a generated visual as the master
identity. Changing the product label while creating marketplace imagery.

**Best Practices:** Maintain one controlled master-logo source. Lock logo components in
templates. Review logo use at final output size. Separate category colour from core logo
integrity. Preserve old versions historically but remove them from active use.

**Chapter Summary:** *"The Muv mark must create recognition through clarity and control. The logo
is not a flexible decoration; it is a protected identifier used consistently across touchpoints
while product and category variation remain subordinate."* Source's own transition line: *"Next:
Language, pronunciation, and messaging ensure the brand sounds as consistent as it looks"* — the
real, sourced justification for why Chapter 3 (Language, Pronunciation & Tagline) follows next in
this domain's frozen chapter sequence.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Pronunciation Standard
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The Founder identified a recurring problem: people read the letters separately as
"M-U-V," while the intended pronunciation is **move**. **Primary Pronunciation: "Muv is
pronounced 'move.'"** Reinforcement is achieved through repetition across real touchpoints:
spoken video and audio; staff and partner training; customer-service introductions; Keep Muving
messaging; pronunciation guidance in internal and franchise material; consistent written casing.

**Identity Rule:** Never solve pronunciation by inventing a new spelling or adding punctuation to
the brand without Founder approval.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Written Identity
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Use **Muv** in customer-facing text where the approved brand form requires a capital
M and lowercase uv. The formal titles of the Knowledge Library and registered systems may
continue to use approved uppercase styling such as MUV Darshan™.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Tone of Voice
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
*"The Muv tone should reflect its personality."*

| Tone Quality | Use | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Clear | Direct sentences and understandable actions | Technical or decorative confusion |
| Warm | Respectful, caring customer language | Forced intimacy |
| Confident | Decisive approved statements | Unsupported certainty |
| Progressive | Language of useful movement | Empty motivational slogans |
| Premium | Controlled rhythm and refined wording | Pretentious vocabulary |
| Practical | Explain what the customer should know or do | Generic filler |

**Founder-Led Directness:** The Founder's communication is often direct — weak work is named as
weak, missing verification is identified, the next step is requested clearly. Customer-facing
language should preserve clarity without copying frustration or internal urgency; internal teams
should be direct about quality while remaining professional and specific.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Messaging System
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Figure 3.1 — Muv Messaging Hierarchy:** Brand meaning → customer relevance → proof or approved
product truth → action.

- **Level 1 — Master Brand Message:** *"Muv supports cleaner, more cared-for living so people can
  Keep Muving."*
- **Level 2 — Category Message:** Explain the approved role of the category (home care, fabric
  care, body care, car care, or another approved area).
- **Level 3 — Product Message:** Use verified product benefits, directions, size, fragrance,
  ingredients, or performance information controlled by the owning product system.
- **Level 4 — Action:** Invite a relevant next step (explore, understand, purchase, enquire, use
  correctly, or continue).

| Message Type | Required Authority |
|---|---|
| Founder philosophy | MUV Darshan™ |
| Brand identity message | MUV Brand Sutra™ |
| Product claim | Product authority |
| Price or offer | Commercial authority |
| Campaign line | Marketing authority |
| Customer-service promise | Operating authority |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Keep Muving™ Philosophy
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Keep Muving is the primary movement expression of the brand. Volume I defines its philosophy;
this section governs its use in identity and messaging.

**Correct Use:** Use it where movement, completion, progress, or continued care is relevant.
Preserve the spelling **Muving**. Maintain approved casing. Use trademark treatment where
formally approved. Let it conclude or reinforce a meaningful experience.

**Incorrect Use:** Repeating it on every page or image. Using it to hide poor customer
experience. Applying it to unrelated claims. Changing the spelling to match generic grammar.
Presenting it as proof of product performance.

**Relationship with "Magic in Muv":** "Magic in Muv" formed part of the earlier product and logo
direction. Later decisions gave Keep Muving stronger brand-wide importance. Existing approved
label use of "Magic in Muv" should not be removed casually; new use must follow the current
identity decision.

**Decision Point:** When an asset contains "Magic in Muv," confirm whether it is a protected
existing label element, an active campaign expression, or historical language before changing it.

**✅ Gap resolved — Founder Decision `FR-008` (2026-07-31):** "Muving Soon™" was flagged as a gap
because it is used in production (the live homepage) and is explicitly named in the Muv AI Sutra
(§6.6, Marketing AI's Brand Language Protection list, as approved teaser language), yet did not
appear anywhere in this chapter's Correct Use / Incorrect Use lists or the Knowledge Library's
searchable text generally — a coverage gap, not a conflict, and one this Knowledge Object
deliberately did not resolve by inference at authoring time.

**The Founder has since ruled directly:** "Muving Soon™" is **approved as an official campaign
teaser**, for: product launch teasers; new fragrance launches; new category launches; website
feature announcements; marketing countdown campaigns. **Restriction:** it must **never replace
"Keep Muving™"** — Keep Muving™ remains the permanent MUV brand philosophy; Muving Soon™ is a
narrower, campaign-scoped teaser expression, not a substitute for or variant of the philosophy
itself. This ruling is now binding and supersedes the prior "open" status — but the original gap
finding is preserved above (not deleted) as the audit trail for how the resolution was reached.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Messaging Checklist
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
- [ ] Muv pronunciation and spelling are correct.
- [ ] The message belongs to the correct authority.
- [ ] Tone is clear, warm, confident, progressive, premium, and practical.
- [ ] Product claims are verified.
- [ ] Keep Muving is relevant rather than repetitive.
- [ ] Historical language is not removed without checking status.
- [ ] The next customer action is clear.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Pronouncing Muv as separate letters. Using uppercase and lowercase
inconsistently. Writing generic luxury language without customer meaning. Turning Keep Muving
into motivational filler. Mixing brand philosophy with unverified product claims.

**Best Practices:** Train pronunciation verbally, not only through documents. Use message
hierarchy before drafting copy. Keep one primary message per asset. Write for clarity before
cleverness. Check every claim with its owning system.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Muv should sound as controlled as it looks. Pronunciation, casing, tone,
message hierarchy, and Keep Muving usage must work together to create a recognisable and
trustworthy voice."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Identity Governance controls
typography, colour, imagery, packaging, and channel consistency"* — the real, sourced
justification for Chapter 4 following next in this domain's frozen sequence.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Typography System
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The Founder repeatedly requested better fonts, clearer text, refined typography, and
consistent casing. **A final named corporate typeface family is not established in the
Foundation evidence.**

**Permanent Typography Principles:** (1) Clarity before decoration. (2) Premium character without
reduced readability. (3) Consistent hierarchy. (4) Correct Muv and Keep Muving casing. (5)
Sufficient size and spacing for the medium. (6) No uncontrolled font substitution.

| Text Role | Required Character |
|---|---|
| Brand headline | Distinctive, refined, highly legible |
| Section heading | Clear hierarchy and confidence |
| Body copy | Comfortable reading across print and digital |
| Product information | Accurate, compact, and legible |
| Legal or mandatory text | Readable at final production size |
| Call to action | Clear and immediately recognisable |

**Decision Point:** A named font becomes permanent only after formal approval, licensing
confirmation, and testing across packaging, digital, marketplace, and document use.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Colour Philosophy
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Colour should support recognition, category navigation, emotion, and premium
character without fragmenting the brand.

**Founder exploration (exploratory, not final):** lavender or purple directions for body care;
pink directions for skin care; emerald green for home care; carbon-gloss orange for car care.
These are evidence-supported category directions, but not a complete final colour specification.

| Layer | Rule |
|---|---|
| Core brand colour | Requires controlled master definition |
| Category colour | Supports navigation without replacing the Muv identity |
| Product colour | Must reflect approved product and packaging truth |
| Background colour | Must preserve logo and text clarity |
| Accent colour | Should guide attention, not dominate |

Do not create permanent colour values from screenshots or generated images. Use approved master
specifications once formally locked.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Iconography & Graphic Language
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The arrow is the primary movement-related graphic idea explored within the identity.
Its exact relationship to the wordmark must remain protected.

**Supporting icons should be:** simple; consistent in weight and style; functional;
understandable at small sizes; subordinate to the Muv mark; free from unsupported meaning.

**Graphic Language should favour:** directional flow; clean space; controlled curves or movement
cues; clear information grouping; category colour used with discipline; premium restraint.
**Avoid:** random sparkles, excessive magic symbolism, inconsistent icon sets, or decorative
arrows that compete with the protected mark.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Photography & Image Style
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The Founder repeatedly asked for realistic, high-quality visuals and instructed that
products must not be altered.

**Photography Principles:** (1) Product form must remain accurate. (2) Labels must remain
unchanged unless revision is explicitly authorized. (3) Product size and height must not be
distorted. (4) Images should feel premium and realistic. (5) The product should remain the
visual truth. (6) Emotional context may support the product but must not fabricate history or
performance. (7) Background and props should fit the category and customer situation.

| Image Type | Required Treatment |
|---|---|
| Product hero | Clear product, accurate label, controlled premium setting |
| Benefit image | Benefit must be approved and visually understandable |
| Lifestyle image | Realistic context without false product behaviour |
| Before/after | Use only when the comparison is truthful and authorized |
| Brand story | Do not introduce unrelated products or invented history |
| Video | Maintain identity consistency across the full sequence |

**Protection Rule:** Never "improve" a product visual by changing the real bottle, label,
colour, size, or approved design.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Packaging Identity Principles
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Detailed packaging production belongs to Volume IV — MUV Design System™. The brand
layer controls identity continuity only.

**Packaging must:** use the approved logo; preserve correct name and tagline treatment; keep
category variation subordinate; maintain product and mandatory information accuracy; avoid
unauthorized label change; remain recognisable across sizes and variants.

| Fixed or Protected | Controlled Variable |
|---|---|
| Approved Muv mark | Category accent |
| Product identity | Variant or fragrance distinction |
| Mandatory information | Supporting imagery |
| Approved label structure | Campaign sticker or secondary panel, if authorized |
| Trademark treatment | Format-specific scaling within approved rules |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Digital Brand Consistency
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Digital interfaces must express the same Muv identity used elsewhere.

**Required controls:** current logo assets; consistent casing and pronunciation; approved
typography hierarchy; controlled colour use; accurate product imagery; approved messaging;
mobile and desktop consistency; reusable components rather than page-by-page reinvention.

Digital motion should reinforce movement without reducing usability or accessibility.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Marketplace Brand Consistency
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Marketplace listings often separate assets from their original design system.
Strong controls are therefore essential.

**Each listing set should maintain:** correct product and label; consistent logo treatment;
accurate title and variant; approved benefit claims; one visual system across hero, benefits,
detail, and story images; no unrelated products in a single-product story; correct price and
pack information; no alteration of real packaging.

**Figure 4.1 — Cross-Touchpoint Consistency Chain:** Master identity → packaging → owned digital
→ marketplace → communication → physical experience.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Identity Change Control
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
When replacing an old logo: (1) identify every active occurrence; (2) confirm the
new approved master; (3) distinguish editable digital assets from printed stock; (4) replace
without altering unrelated content; (5) verify every output; (6) record what remains in
transition; (7) prevent the old logo from returning through templates or stored assets.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Creating permanent font or colour rules from generated output. Using
category colour as a substitute for the main identity. Mixing icon styles. Altering a product
while creating a "better" image. Updating one digital page while leaving old identity elsewhere.
Producing marketplace assets without checking packaging truth.

**Best Practices:** Maintain controlled master assets. Separate fixed identity from category
expression. Test typography and colour in final-size conditions. Use reusable digital and
marketplace templates. Audit old identity across every channel after a change.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Confirm master logo and current version.
- [ ] Check typography hierarchy and casing.
- [ ] Use only approved colour specifications.
- [ ] Verify icon consistency.
- [ ] Confirm image realism and product accuracy.
- [ ] Protect packaging elements.
- [ ] Check digital components across devices.
- [ ] Review the full marketplace image set.
- [ ] Record transitional old-identity occurrences.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Identity Governance converts brand intention into repeatable control.
Typography, colour, graphics, photography, packaging, digital, and marketplace expression may
vary by context, but they must remain subordinate to one protected Muv identity."* Source's own
transition line: *"Next: Brand Decision History establishes how identity changes are approved,
preserved, and protected"* — the sourced justification for Chapter 5 following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Decision History
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Muv's identity evolved through real alternatives. The early **Muv.a** direction was
rejected. Instructions later included removal of ".a," revision of logo treatments, replacement
of old logos, addition of TM, and changing the relationship between the logo and supporting
language. These changes demonstrate that an idea's presence in historical work does not make it
active.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Identity Decision States
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| State | Meaning | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Proposed | Suggested but not approved | Evaluate only |
| Exploratory | Being compared or visualised | Test without standardising |
| Qualified | Partly accepted; details remain open | Apply only settled elements |
| Approved | Explicitly chosen | Implement within scope |
| Deferred | Preserved for later decision | Do not activate |
| Rejected | Stopped | Keep outside active use |
| Superseded | Replaced by a later approved state | Preserve historically |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Internal Brand Governance
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Authority:** The Founder remains the final authority for Founder philosophy and major identity
decisions. Teams may apply approved standards but cannot silently create new permanent identity
rules.

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Founder | Final identity authority |
| Brand custodian | Maintains approved standards and master assets |
| Designer or agency | Creates within the approved system |
| Product and packaging team | Preserves identity while applying product truth |
| Digital team | Implements consistent reusable components |
| Marketplace team | Applies accurate templates and claims |
| Reviewer | Verifies consistency and decision status |

**Figure 5.1 — Brand Approval Path:** Brief → authority check → concept → application test →
Founder review where required → approval → master update → rollout → audit.

**Every identity decision should record:** what changed; why it changed; what remains fixed;
where it applies; approval state; effective version; old assets to retire; dependent systems to
update.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Protection Rules
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Master Asset Protection:** Maintain one authoritative source for active brand assets. Restrict
editing of master logos. Use export files appropriate to the medium. Do not recreate master
assets from screenshots.

**Terminology Protection:** Write Muv according to the approved customer-facing form. Pronounce
it "move." Preserve Keep Muving spelling. Use trademark symbols only in the approved manner. Do
not reintroduce rejected naming such as Muv.a.

**Visual Protection:** Do not distort the logo. Do not alter product labels without instruction.
Do not use inconsistent category treatments. Do not allow generated imagery to change product
truth. Do not combine old and new active identity.

**Message Protection:** Do not invent Founder philosophy. Do not invent product claims. Do not
promise guarantees without operating authority. Do not use Keep Muving as filler. Do not confuse
historical language with active messaging.

**Channel Protection:** Update owned digital components from master assets. Audit marketplace
listing sets. Control vendor and agency files. Train staff and partners in pronunciation.
Preserve approved files for future franchise use.

**Warning:** Small uncontrolled differences become a second identity when repeated across enough
touchpoints.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Exception Process
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
When a standard cannot be followed: (1) state the exact constraint; (2) identify the
protected principle; (3) propose the smallest exception; (4) show the exception in real
application; (5) obtain the required approval; (6) record whether the exception is one-time or
permanent; (7) do not convert a one-time exception into a template.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Audit Checklist
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
- [ ] Current logo used everywhere.
- [ ] Old logo occurrences identified.
- [ ] Muv spelling and pronunciation correct.
- [ ] Keep Muving treatment consistent.
- [ ] Typography follows approved hierarchy.
- [ ] Colours follow controlled specifications.
- [ ] Product imagery remains accurate.
- [ ] Packaging is not altered.
- [ ] Digital components use master assets.
- [ ] Marketplace sets remain consistent.
- [ ] Claims belong to the correct authority.
- [ ] Exceptions are documented.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Treating an old file as current because it is easy to find. Allowing a
vendor to create a new logo version. Failing to update templates after approval. Applying a
one-time exception across the system. Removing decision history and later repeating rejected
work.

**Best Practices:** Version every major identity release. Retain historical files outside
active-use folders. Audit all dependent channels after change. Train people in both rules and
reasons. Treat approval and rollout as separate stages.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Brand protection is the discipline of keeping one identity intact across
people, tools, channels, and time. Muv's history must remain preserved, but only the latest
approved state may govern active expression."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Volume IV
converts identity into the detailed MUV Design System™ for packaging, labels, assets, and
production"* — confirming Part III (this domain's real source) ends here; Part IV is explicitly
out of Domain 1's scope, never pulled in.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Design Philosophy & Foundation
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
MUV Darshan™ establishes why the brand exists. MUV Brand Sutra™ establishes how
the identity must be understood and protected. MUV Design System™ converts those decisions
into visible, usable assets.

**Figure 1.1 — Philosophy-to-Production Chain:** MUV Darshan™ → MUV Brand Sutra™ → MUV Design
System™ → Production Asset → Customer Touchpoint.

| System | Governing Question |
|---|---|
| MUV Darshan™ | Why should this exist? |
| MUV Brand Sutra™ | How must it remain recognisably Muv? |
| MUV Design System™ | How should it be designed and produced correctly? |
| Production | Can the approved design be manufactured or published accurately? |
| Customer touchpoint | Can the customer understand and trust it? |

Design is not independent authorship. It is controlled translation.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Recognition before Decoration & Role of Design in Customer Trust
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. the Muv identity; 2. the product type; 3. the
variant or fragrance; 4. the most important approved information; 5. the required action or
usage context. Decorative effects come after recognition and comprehension.

> **DESIGN RULE** — If an effect makes the logo, product type, variant, or mandatory
> information harder to understand, it is not premium.

**Packaging makes several silent promises:** the product is what it claims to be; the company
has controlled its information; the pack belongs to the same brand as other Muv products; the
customer can understand how to use it; the physical item should match the image used to sell
it. Inconsistent spelling, distorted bottles, incorrect labels, unclear variants, or missing
information weaken trust before the product is used.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Packaging System Model
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Master identity → category → product →
variant → size → front label → back label → production file.

| Level | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Master identity | Maintains Muv recognition |
| Category | Distinguishes home, fabric, body, car, or another approved area |
| Product | Identifies the product type |
| Variant | Distinguishes fragrance, formulation, or approved option |
| Size | Distinguishes volume or pack format |
| Front label | Supports immediate recognition and selection |
| Back label | Provides use, product, company, and mandatory information |
| Production file | Converts the approved design into printable dimensions and specifications |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Bottle and Packaging Philosophy
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The container must support the product and the customer before it supports
decoration. **Evaluate:** suitability for the product; handling and pouring; closure or pump
function; size and proportion; label area; transport and storage; shelf recognition;
photography and marketplace presentation; production availability. The Founder explored
multiple bottle, cap, pump, shape, and size presentations. Those explorations do not create a
universal container rule. The approved physical pack for each product remains the production
truth.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Category Differentiation & Variant System
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Volume III records early category-colour directions, including lavender or purple
for body care, pink for skin care, emerald green for home care, and carbon-gloss orange for car
care. These directions must be applied only through controlled specifications.

| Fixed Layer | Controlled Variable |
|---|---|
| Muv identity | Category accent |
| Product-name hierarchy | Variant colour or cue |
| Approved label structure | Supporting imagery |
| Mandatory information zones | Size-specific spacing |
| Product truth | Approved fragrance distinction |

Category differentiation should make navigation easier without creating separate brands.

**Variant System — variants need a repeatable pattern:** 1. stable product family; 2. clear
variant name; 3. controlled colour or visual cue; 4. consistent placement; 5. accurate size; 6.
no conflict with core identity.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Size and Format Consistency & Design Thinking Framework
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
preserve hierarchy; adapt spacing deliberately; maintain
readable mandatory text; confirm barcode and production areas; check curves, seams, handles,
pumps, and caps; test the artwork at physical size.

**Figure 1.3 — The Muv Design Thinking Framework:** Truth → Purpose → Hierarchy → Expression →
Production → Verification.

| Stage | Required Question |
|---|---|
| Truth | What is the approved product, pack, identity, and information? |
| Purpose | What must the customer understand or do? |
| Hierarchy | What should be seen first, second, and third? |
| Expression | How can the design feel premium and recognisably Muv? |
| Production | Can it be created accurately in the required format? |
| Verification | Does the output match the approved physical and informational truth? |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Production Discipline
Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Designing before confirming the real container. Stretching one label
across different sizes. Using category colour as the main identity. Sending a visual mockup as
a printer-ready file. Treating generated dimensions as production truth.

**Best Practices:** Start with a physical pack specification. Build a master hierarchy before
creating variants. Test labels on the actual bottle. Separate concept approval from production
approval. Maintain a controlled format matrix.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Confirm product and container.
- [ ] Confirm category, variant, and size.
- [ ] Use the current Muv identity.
- [ ] Establish hierarchy.
- [ ] Check format-specific constraints.
- [ ] Prepare production specifications.
- [ ] Review a physical-size proof.
- [ ] Record the approved version.

**Key Takeaways:** Design begins with recognition, customer trust, and product truth.
Packaging must operate as a coherent architecture, not as isolated artwork. Category, variant,
and size differences must remain controlled and recognisably Muv. Production feasibility is
part of design quality.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Packaging Architecture turns one Muv identity into a scalable physical
system. It protects recognition while allowing controlled differences across categories,
variants, and sizes."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: The Label Information System
defines exactly how product and company information should be organised"* — the sourced
justification for Chapter 2 following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Label Hierarchy
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Brand → product type → variant → approved
benefit → size → use information → company and mandatory information. The front and back label
perform different jobs.

**Front Label** should help the customer recognise and select the product. **Typical
hierarchy:** 1. Muv identity; 2. product type; 3. variant or fragrance; 4. one or more approved
primary benefits; 5. net quantity; 6. required mark or category cue.

**Back Label** should help the customer understand, use, identify, and contact. **Possible
information includes:** short approved description; directions for use; precautions or
warnings; ingredients or composition where approved and required; manufacturer and marketer
information; customer-care details; website and email; net quantity; batch, manufacturing,
expiry, or best-before fields where applicable; MRP field; barcode area; mandatory
declarations.

> **WARNING** — The presence, wording, and legal form of mandatory information must be
> confirmed by the appropriate compliance authority. Design cannot invent compliance.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Product Information Structure
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Information Type | Governing Source |
|---|---|
| Brand name and mark | MUV Brand Sutra™ |
| Product name | Approved product record |
| Variant or fragrance | Approved product record |
| Benefit or performance claim | Product and compliance authority |
| Directions | Approved product-use instruction |
| Ingredients | Approved formulation and compliance information |
| Price | Commercial authority |
| Company and contact details | Current company record |
| Barcode | Assigned operational record |
| Dimensions | Measured production specification |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Claims Control
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
A label is not the place to create persuasive claims first and validate them
later. **For each claim, record:** exact wording; supporting product basis; approval owner;
applicable variant and size; legal or marketplace constraints; effective version. Do not
convert a general brand promise into a measurable product claim.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: MRP and Variable Information
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Pricing and variable production fields require disciplined placement. The Founder
corrected MRP placement and distinguished front-label presentation from back-label changes.
This demonstrates a permanent rule:

> Change the requested field in the requested location. Do not use a price correction as
> permission to redesign unrelated elements.

Variable-data zones should remain clear enough for production printing, stamping, or stickers.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Dimensions and Measured Artwork & Editable Production Files
Sticker System & Label Approval Gate
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Stickers may support variable information, temporary promotion, or controlled
updates. They must not become a substitute for fixing the master artwork when a permanent
change is required.

| Sticker Use | Control |
|---|---|
| Variable price or batch information | Must align with the production process |
| Temporary promotion | Requires start and end control |
| Corrective application | Must be authorized and accurately positioned |
| Brand or benefit sticker | Must not obscure mandatory information |

**Label Approval Gate:**
- [ ] Correct product, variant, and size.
- [ ] Current logo and identity.
- [ ] Front hierarchy is clear.
- [ ] Back information is complete.
- [ ] Claims are approved.
- [ ] MRP and variable zones are correct.
- [ ] Company details are current.
- [ ] Barcode space is usable.
- [ ] Dimensions match the real pack.
- [ ] Physical-size proof is readable.
- [ ] Editable and exported files match.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Inventing ingredients or claims during design. Copying information from
another size or variant without checking. Changing front and back information inconsistently.
Supplying screenshots instead of editable production files. Using stickers without a removal or
transition plan.

**Best Practices:** Maintain a controlled product-information sheet. Separate fixed and
variable information. Use a label-content approval before visual approval. Proof at actual
size. Keep one approved production package per version.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Verify the product-information source.
- [ ] Confirm front, back, and variable-information zones.
- [ ] Confirm every claim and mandatory detail.
- [ ] Match artwork dimensions to the measured production pack.
- [ ] Check readability at physical size.
- [ ] Align the editable master with the exported proof.
- [ ] Record the approved version.

**Key Takeaways:** A label is an information system before it is a decorative surface. Product
facts, claims, dimensions, and variable data require controlled sources. Front and back labels
must operate as one coordinated system. Approval requires both content accuracy and production
readiness.

**Chapter Summary:** *"The Label Information System converts product truth into a clear
customer and production structure. Its quality depends on hierarchy, accurate sources,
measured dimensions, and controlled files—not on visual appearance alone."* Source's own
transition line: *"Next: Visual Asset Production governs how the real product is represented in
photography, e-commerce, and customer communication"* — the sourced justification for Chapter 3
following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Product Truth Protection & Product Image System
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The Founder repeatedly gave a direct constraint: *"Do not change anything in the
bottle, label, size, or height."* This is the first rule of product imagery. Visual enhancement
may improve lighting, background, composition, sharpness, or context. It may not replace the
real product with an attractive fiction.

**Figure 3.1 — Product Image System:** Truth image → hero image → benefit image → detail image
→ how-to image → lifestyle image → comparison image → brand-story image.

| Image Type | Primary Purpose |
|---|---|
| Truth image | Establish the accurate product reference |
| Hero image | Present the product clearly and attractively |
| Benefit image | Explain an approved benefit |
| Close-up image | Show label, texture, closure, or relevant detail |
| How-to image | Explain approved usage |
| Lifestyle image | Place the product in a realistic customer context |
| Before/after image | Show a truthful authorized comparison |
| Brand-story image | Connect the product to approved brand meaning |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Photography Standards
Hero Images
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. What is the product? 2.
Which Muv product or variant is it? 3. Why should the customer continue exploring? Avoid
overcrowding the hero with every benefit, badge, prop, and claim.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Lifestyle Images
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Lifestyle imagery may add emotional relevance. It should depict a plausible use
environment without creating false product performance or fake Founder history. For example,
car-care communication explored emotional connection with Indian family cars. The emotional
context may support the product; it cannot substitute for accurate specifications or verified
performance.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Benefit Images & Close-Up Images
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
one approved benefit; a clear product
relationship; concise language; a visual explanation that does not overclaim; consistent brand
treatment.

**Use close-ups to clarify:** label information; texture or consistency where truthful;
closure or pump; fragrance or variant cue; relevant pack detail. Do not enlarge or sharpen
details until they no longer resemble the real product.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: How-to-Use Visuals
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Prepare → apply or dose → use correctly →
complete → store safely. The exact sequence belongs to the product authority. Design is
responsible for clarity, order, and visual comprehension.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Before/After Visuals
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Before/after imagery carries high trust risk. **Use only when:** the comparison is
representative and authorized; conditions are not misleading; the product and method are
accurate; the result is not digitally fabricated; required qualifications are visible.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Marketplace Image Standards
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. clean primary product image;
2. key benefits; 3. product or label detail; 4. usage; 5. variant or fragrance; 6. approved
comparison; 7. brand story. The Founder specifically corrected brand-story imagery that
introduced other products when only the uploaded product should appear.

> **DESIGN RULE** — A single-product listing should not become a mixed-product advertisement
> unless the asset purpose explicitly requires it.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: AI-Generated Asset Governance
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
AI may help create backgrounds, compositions, lighting concepts, or contextual
scenes. It must not be trusted to preserve the product automatically. **For every generated
asset:** compare the bottle with the truth image; compare the label character by character
where readable; verify cap, pump, colour, size, and shape; inspect hands, reflections, text,
edges, and background objects; reject invented products or variants; retain the approved source
product layer where possible.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Replacing a real label with generated text. Changing bottle proportions.
Showing unapproved benefits. Using low-resolution output for marketplace zoom. Inserting
unrelated products into a single-product story. Treating a beautiful image as accurate without
comparison.

**Best Practices:** Build every set from one truth image. Use a defined image sequence. Keep
one primary message per image. Compare generated output at high zoom. Verify the complete
listing as a system.

**Visual Asset Checklist:**
- [ ] Product matches the truth image.
- [ ] Label is unchanged.
- [ ] Bottle proportions are correct.
- [ ] Image purpose is clear.
- [ ] Claim is approved.
- [ ] Resolution and ratio suit the channel.
- [ ] Background is clean and realistic.
- [ ] Brand treatment is consistent.
- [ ] Product set contains no unintended items.
- [ ] Final output has been reviewed at full size.

**Key Takeaways:** Every product visual must remain faithful to the real approved product.
Different image types have different roles in the customer decision journey. Marketplace and
digital optimisation cannot override accuracy. AI can assist production, but it cannot become
the source of product truth.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Visual Asset Production exists to make the real product easier to
understand and more desirable without changing its truth. Accuracy is the foundation; premium
composition builds on top of it."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: 3D Visualization &
Mockups defines how concepts and applications may be simulated without becoming false
production records"* — the sourced justification for Chapter 4 following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Role of a Mockup
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
A mockup allows a concept, packaging idea, or digital layout to be visualised
before it is finalised. It helps the Founder and team evaluate an idea in a realistic context
without committing to full production. A mockup is a communication tool, not a production
record.

> **WARNING** — Never use a mockup as the only source for dimensions, product facts, or print
> production.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: 3D Visualization Standard
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
concept brief → base model → material and
finish pass → label and identity application → lighting and environment → render → Founder or
authority review → approved for use / return for revision.

**Review at every stage:** does the 3D model match the actual product dimensions; is the label
artwork the current approved version; are materials, finishes, and colours accurate; is the cap,
pump, or closure represented correctly; is the render resolution sufficient for its intended use;
is the lighting realistic rather than artificially flattering in a misleading way; does the
render avoid implying features, size, or claims the physical product does not have; is the file
clearly labelled as a render, not a photograph, where the distinction matters; has the render
been compared against a real product reference.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Concept versus Final
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Dimension | Concept | Final |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Explore and communicate an idea | Represent the approved, production-accurate product |
| Approval status | Not yet approved | Founder or authority approved |
| Accuracy requirement | Directionally accurate | Fully accurate in every detail |
| Usage | Internal discussion, early-stage pitch | Customer-facing, marketplace, print |
| Labelling | Should be marked as concept/draft | Carries no draft marking |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Digital Design System
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. colour tokens; 2. typography scale; 3. button
system; 4. iconography set; 5. spacing and grid system; 6. card and container components; 7.
form and input styling; 8. navigation components; 9. imagery and thumbnail treatment; 10.
motion and interaction principles.

**Ownership note (source-native):** these components are defined creatively in this chapter,
but their technical build and governance are owned by Volume II's Enterprise Operating System
and website architecture material — this chapter does not redefine or duplicate that ownership,
only the creative-design intent.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: UI Consistency
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Element | Consistency Requirement |
|---|---|
| Colour usage | Matches approved brand palette across every screen |
| Typography | Same type scale and hierarchy across every screen |
| Button behaviour | Same shape, state, and interaction logic everywhere |
| Iconography | Same icon set and stroke weight throughout |
| Spacing | Same grid and spacing rhythm across pages |
| Imagery treatment | Same crop, filter, and framing logic across the site |
| Tone of microcopy | Same brand voice in every UI text element |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Journey Visuals & Website Imagery
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
discovery visual → consideration visual →
decision visual → purchase visual → post-purchase visual — each stage supported by imagery
suited to the customer's mindset at that stage.

**Website Imagery — should include:** 1. homepage hero imagery; 2. category-level imagery; 3.
product-level imagery (aligned with Chapter 3's product image system); 4. lifestyle and brand
storytelling imagery; 5. trust and credibility imagery; 6. educational or how-to imagery; 7.
banner and promotional imagery.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Social Media Design Principles
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. remain instantly identifiable as Muv even without
a logo visible; 2. adapt to each platform's native format rather than forcing one format
everywhere; 3. prioritise legibility at small size; 4. use consistent colour and type treatment
across posts; 5. balance brand consistency with platform-native creative trends; 6. avoid
overcrowding a single post with too many messages; 7. maintain the same product-truth standard
as any other channel.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: AI-Generated Asset Governance (3D/Mockup/UI)
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. confirm the asset is clearly
labelled as AI-assisted where that distinction matters; 2. verify no invented product features,
dimensions, or claims have been introduced; 3. check brand colour, typography, and identity
elements against the approved system; 4. review for visual artefacts, distortions, or
inconsistencies typical of generated imagery; 5. confirm the asset does not imply a capability,
certification, or claim the product does not have; 6. route any customer-facing use through
Founder or authority review before publication; 7. retain a record of the prompt or generation
method used, where practical, for future accountability.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Treating a concept render as a final production reference. Using a mockup
to justify a customer-facing dimension or specification claim. Allowing an AI-generated render
to introduce features the physical product lacks. Letting social and website imagery drift from
the approved brand system over time. Skipping Founder or authority review before publishing a
generated asset. Mixing draft and final assets in the same customer-facing set without labelling.

**Best Practices:** Label every concept and draft asset clearly. Compare every 3D render against
a real product reference before approval. Maintain one shared Digital Design System across web,
social, and app surfaces. Review AI-generated assets against the same standard as any other
asset. Keep a record of what was generated, how, and by whom.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Mockup or render is not being used as the sole source of product facts.
- [ ] 3D model dimensions match the physical product.
- [ ] Label artwork on the render is the current approved version.
- [ ] Concept assets are clearly marked as concept, not final.
- [ ] Digital Design System components are used consistently.
- [ ] UI elements match across all screens and surfaces.
- [ ] Website and social imagery align with the approved brand system.
- [ ] AI-generated 3D/mockup/UI assets have passed the seven-step governance check.
- [ ] Founder or authority has reviewed any customer-facing generated asset.

**Key Takeaways:** A mockup communicates an idea; it does not certify a fact. Concept and final
assets must never be interchanged. One Digital Design System keeps web, social, and app
experiences coherent. AI can accelerate 3D, mockup, and UI production, but every generated
asset still answers to the same product-truth and brand standard as a photograph.

**Chapter Summary:** *"3D Visualization & Mockups exists to let ideas be explored and
communicated safely, without ever becoming an unverified substitute for the real, approved
product."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Design Controls & Revision History defines how
design work is requested, revised, approved, and preserved over time"* — the sourced
justification for Chapter 5 following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Founder-Led Revision Pattern
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. correcting a brand-story image that
introduced other products when only the uploaded product should appear; 2. requiring
lifestyle imagery to reflect a plausible Indian family-car context rather than a generic
stock scene; 3. instructing that mockups never substitute for verified product dimensions;
4. requiring marketplace image sets to avoid becoming mixed-product advertisements; 5.
correcting overclaiming in benefit visuals; 6. requiring before/after imagery to meet all
five trust conditions before use; 7. requiring AI-generated assets to be verified against
the truth image before approval; 8. requiring design revisions to stay within the original
brief's scope rather than expanding into a new concept.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Design Workflow
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. brief received; 2. brief
clarified with requester; 3. concept development; 4. internal design review; 5. Founder or
authority review; 6. revision cycle (if required); 7. final approval; 8. asset production;
9. asset filed and versioned; 10. asset released for use.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Design Brief
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Requester | Who is asking for the asset |
| Purpose | Why the asset is needed |
| Audience | Who will see it |
| Channel | Where it will be used |
| Key message | The single primary message |
| Mandatory elements | What must appear (logo, MRP, compliance text, etc.) |
| Reference assets | Prior work or examples to align with |
| Tone | The intended emotional register |
| Deadline | When it is needed |
| Approval authority | Who signs off |
| Success criteria | How the asset will be judged |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Revision Control
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. version number; 2. date of revision; 3. requested
by; 4. reason for revision; 5. specific change requested; 6. reviewer; 7. approval status;
8. prior version reference; 9. final version confirmation.

> **DESIGN RULE** — A revision request is not permission to redesign the entire asset.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Asset Management
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Practice | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Naming convention | Consistent, descriptive file names across all assets |
| Version control | Every asset traceable to its revision history |
| Central storage | One authoritative location for approved assets |
| Access control | Only authorised roles can publish or replace approved assets |
| Archive policy | Superseded assets retained, not deleted |
| Format standards | Correct file types and specifications for each channel |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Designer and Vendor Guidelines
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. work from the current approved brief, not an
outdated one; 2. use only current approved brand and product assets as reference; 3. flag any
ambiguity before proceeding rather than assuming; 4. submit work through the defined review
stages, not directly to publication; 5. respect revision scope as defined in the brief; 6.
maintain confidentiality of unreleased product and brand material; 7. deliver in the agreed
file formats and specifications; 8. accept that Founder or authority approval is final.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Design Audit
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
packaging, label, website, marketplace listings, social
media, email/newsletter, print collateral, in-store or trade material, mockups/renders in
active use, third-party vendor material.

**The ten check items applied per channel:** 1. current approved version in use; 2. brand
colour and typography correct; 3. logo usage correct; 4. mandatory information present and
accurate; 5. no unapproved claims present; 6. imagery meets product-truth standard; 7. no
superseded assets still live; 8. file quality sufficient for the channel; 9. consistent
treatment across the channel; 10. audit findings logged and routed for correction.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Treating a revision request as licence to redesign the whole asset.
Skipping the brief and working from memory of a past version. Publishing before Founder or
authority approval. Losing track of which version is current. Allowing vendors to work from
outdated references. Failing to archive superseded assets. Auditing inconsistently or not at
all.

**Best Practices:** Always start from a written brief. Track every revision with a reason.
Maintain one central, access-controlled asset library. Hold external vendors to the same
standard as internal designers. Run the Design Audit on a regular cadence, not only when a
problem is noticed. Treat Founder approval as the final gate, not a formality. Archive, never
delete, superseded work.

**Future Scalability:** As the design volume grows, expect: more designers and vendors working
in parallel; more channels requiring simultaneous consistency; more revision cycles running
concurrently; a growing need for a searchable central asset library; a growing need for
role-based access control; potential need for a dedicated design-operations function; growing
importance of the Design Audit as a scaling mechanism; growing reliance on AI-assisted
production requiring the same governance discipline at higher volume.

**Final Design Approval Checklist:**
- [ ] Brief is complete and approved before work begins.
- [ ] Concept aligns with the brief's key message and mandatory elements.
- [ ] Internal design review completed.
- [ ] Founder or authority review completed.
- [ ] All revision requests stayed within the brief's original scope.
- [ ] Final version is clearly marked and distinguished from prior versions.
- [ ] Asset filed in the central, version-controlled library.
- [ ] Asset meets the format and quality standard for its channel.
- [ ] Mandatory information is present and accurate.
- [ ] No unapproved claims are present.
- [ ] Vendor or external designer work meets internal standard.
- [ ] Asset has passed the Design Audit for its channel.

**Key Takeaways:** Design work moves through a defined, repeatable workflow, not an ad hoc
process. Revision exists to refine within scope, not to reopen the whole concept. Asset
management and the Design Audit are what keep consistency intact as volume grows. Founder or
authority approval remains the final gate at every stage of scale.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Design Controls & Revision History exists to make sure creative
quality does not depend on memory or goodwill — it depends on a defined, auditable system that
holds as the team and channel count grow."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Part V — MUV
Product Sutra™"* — noted for completeness; Part V is out of scope for Domain 6.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Part IV Part Summary: MUV Design System in One View
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Chapter | Core Governing Idea |
|---|---|
| 1. Packaging Architecture | Premium effects must never obscure logo, product type, variant, or mandatory information |
| 2. Label Information System | Compliance authority confirms presence, wording, and legal form of mandatory information; design cannot invent compliance |
| 3. Visual Asset Production | Never change the bottle, label, size, or height; visual enhancement supports truth, never replaces it |
| 4. 3D Visualization & Mockups | A mockup communicates an idea; it never certifies a fact |
| 5. Design Controls & Revision History | A revision refines within scope; it is never permission to redesign |
| Category Differentiation | Category colour direction distinguishes product lines without breaking brand unity |
| Digital Design System | One shared system of components keeps web, social, and app experiences coherent |
| AI-Generated Asset Governance (packaging/photography) | AI may assist production; it cannot become the source of product truth |
| AI-Generated Asset Governance (3D/mockup/UI) | Every generated 3D, mockup, or UI asset answers to the same standard as a photograph |
| Design Workflow | Ten defined stages, not an ad hoc process |
| Asset Management | One central, version-controlled, access-controlled library |
| Design Audit | Ten channels, ten checks, run on a regular cadence |

**Master Design Principles:** 1. The real, approved product is the single source of truth. 2.
Compliance content is confirmed by authority, never invented by design. 3. Premium execution
never obscures required clarity. 4. Concept and final are never interchangeable. 5. Every
generated or rendered asset is verified against a truth reference before use. 6. One shared
design system holds every digital surface together. 7. Revision refines; it does not reopen.
8. Every asset is version-controlled and traceable. 9. External vendors meet the same standard
as internal designers. 10. Consistency is maintained by a recurring audit, not by memory.

**Master Design Checklist:**
- [ ] Product truth preserved in every packaging and visual asset.
- [ ] Mandatory information confirmed by compliance authority, not invented.
