- [ ] Premium effects tested against the "harder to understand" rule.
- [ ] Category differentiation applied without breaking brand unity.
- [ ] Every AI-generated asset passed its applicable governance protocol.
- [ ] Mockups and renders never used as the sole source of product facts.
- [ ] Digital Design System components used consistently across web, social, and app.
- [ ] UI consistency held across every screen.
- [ ] Website and social imagery aligned with the approved brand system.
- [ ] Every design brief complete and approved before work began.
- [ ] Every revision stayed within its original scope.
- [ ] Every asset filed in the central, version-controlled library.
- [ ] Design Audit passed for every active channel.
- [ ] Founder or authority approval obtained as the final gate.

**Part End Note (source-native, preserved for completeness):** Part IV closes here. *"Next:
Part V — MUV Product Sutra™"* — out of scope for Domain 6; noted only as the source's own
transition, not acted upon.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Experience Philosophy
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Figure 1.1 — Customer Experience Philosophy:** Promise → Interaction →
Product/service reality → Customer interpretation → Trust or friction → Company learning →
Improved promise and delivery.

Customer experience is created through: product quality; communication; purchase journey;
delivery; usage experience; support; problem resolution; continuous improvement. No single
department controls all of these — every function owns the consequences of its decisions.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Brand Promise & Customer Reality
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Volume III defines what Muv represents. Customer experience reveals whether that
meaning survives contact with reality.

| Promise source | Customer reality |
|---|---|
| Brand language | How communication feels and whether it remains clear |
| Product claim | What the product actually delivers in correct use |
| Design | Whether customers can recognise, understand, and use the product |
| Price/value | Whether the choice feels fair and supportable |
| Sales promise | Whether terms, availability, and delivery match |
| Service promise | Whether the customer is heard and helped |
| Company values | How Muv behaves when something goes wrong |

**Customer Experience Rule:** Never judge the experience only from company intent. Judge it from
the customer's complete observed reality and verified evidence.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Trust as an Asset
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Trust accumulates when Muv: says what is true; delivers what was agreed; makes
products and information consistent; respects customer time and dignity; communicates early
when reality changes; resolves problems fairly; remembers learning. Trust can be damaged by one
high-severity failure or by repeated minor friction.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer-First Thinking (Company-Wide Version)
Customer Journey Map & Journey Mapping
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The experience begins before purchase and continues after product use.

**Figure 1.2 — Muv Customer Journey Map:**

| Stage | Customer question | Muv responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Awareness | Is this relevant to me? | Communicate a real problem and value |
| Discovery | What is Muv and what does it offer? | Make identity and range understandable |
| Evaluation | Is this right and trustworthy? | Provide accurate product, price, proof, use, and support |
| Purchase | Can I buy confidently and easily? | Ensure clear choice, terms, payment, and availability |
| Delivery | Will the right product arrive correctly? | Fulfil accurately, safely, and transparently |
| First use | How do I use it and what should I expect? | Provide guidance and reachable help |
| Ongoing use | Does it remain valuable and consistent? | Deliver product truth and learning support |
| Repeat | Is it worth choosing again? | Reinforce value, availability, and trust |
| Loyalty | Does Muv understand and respect me? | Build continuity without pressure |
| Advocacy | Should I recommend Muv? | Enable authentic sharing and protect reputation |

**Journey Mapping — for each journey, document:** customer type; objective; stages; touchpoints;
customer questions; expected experience; owner; evidence/system dependency; friction; failure
and escalation; measurement; improvement. Journey maps must reflect actual channels and
behaviour, not an idealised diagram.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Moments of Truth
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
A moment of truth materially affects trust: first recognition of the brand; first
product comparison; payment; order confirmation; delivery delay or damage; opening the pack;
first use; complaint response; refund/replacement; repeat availability. These moments deserve
explicit standards and ownership.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Experience Ownership & Handoff Ownership
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Function | Customer-experience responsibility |
|---|---|
| Brand | Promise, identity, language, recognition |
| Product | Product objective, performance, use, claims |
| Design | Understandable and accurate physical/digital expression |
| Manufacturing/quality | Consistent product and traceable problem evidence |
| Marketing | Relevant expectation and education |
| Sales/distribution | Accurate terms, availability, fulfilment, and handoff |
| Customer support | Listening, response, ownership, resolution, and records |
| Technology | Reliable, accessible, understandable digital interaction |
| Leadership | Cross-functional priorities, authority, and improvement |

**Handoff Ownership** — the customer should not have to understand Muv's organisation. When a
request moves between teams: the current owner explains the next step; essential context
travels with the case; a named receiving owner accepts it; the customer receives a realistic
time/next update; no one asks the customer to repeat avoidable information.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Experience Standards, Founder Note & Decision Points
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
An experience standard should define: intended outcome; scope and channel;
responsible owner; behaviour or process; information required; response or completion
expectation; exception and escalation; record; measure. This volume does not invent unsupported
numeric response-time commitments — such standards require operational approval and capacity.

**Founder Note:** The recovered experience architecture includes customer-facing food-service,
outlet, menu/product, culture, franchise, and communication evidence. It must be used as
evidence of experience design — not as permission to invent customer stories, satisfaction
results, or universal claims.

**Decision Points, when an experience improvement is proposed:** Is the problem verified? Which
journey and customers are affected? Is the root cause understood? Which function owns it? What
standard or system changes? How will improvement be validated?

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Calling support the complete customer experience. Designing journeys from
internal departments. Treating a completed transaction as a successful relationship. Promising
response levels without operational capacity. Solving one complaint without finding repeated
friction. Measuring only satisfaction after the fact.

**Best Practices:** Map real journeys by customer and channel. Give every moment of truth an
owner. Review handoffs. Combine customer voice with operational evidence. Design for normal use
and failure recovery. Preserve learning across teams.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Customer and journey objective defined.
- [ ] Promise and expected reality aligned.
- [ ] All stages and touchpoints mapped.
- [ ] Moments of truth identified.
- [ ] Owners and handoffs explicit.
- [ ] Standards and escalation paths approved.
- [ ] Customer effort and dignity considered.
- [ ] Evidence and measurement plan defined.
- [ ] Improvement decision and owner recorded.

**Key Takeaways:** Customer experience is the company-wide result of promise and execution.
Trust grows through consistent truth, respect, and recovery. The journey extends from awareness
through advocacy. Handoffs must be invisible in effort but visible in ownership.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Customer Promise & Experience Context establishes Muv's customer-first
system. It connects the brand promise to every real interaction and assigns experience ownership
across the company."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Food-Service Product Experience
governs the product, purchase, delivery, first-use, and repeat-use reality customers receive"* —
the sourced justification for Chapter 2 following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Product Experience, Product Truth & Choice Architecture
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The customer experiences a product as one system: **Need → Selection →
Expectation → Purchase → Receipt → Opening/presentation → Use/consumption → Result → Memory.**

**Figure 2.1 — Product Experience Chain:**

| Experience area | Customer expectation |
|---|---|
| Product choice | Understandable category, variant, size, and suitability |
| Information | Accurate benefits, use, price, ingredients/details where applicable |
| Availability | Product shown can be obtained |
| Receipt | Correct, intact, clean, and identifiable item |
| First impression | Pack/product/presentation matches expectation |
| Use/consumption | Directions, format, performance, sensory experience |
| Value | Outcome and experience justify total cost and effort |
| Support | Questions and problems have a clear route |

**Product Truth in Experience:** Volume V and Volume VI own technical product truth and
quality. CX ensures that truth is correctly understood and experienced. **Never:** recommend the
wrong product to close a sale; conceal usage limitations; show a pack or presentation unlike the
delivered product; promise a performance or time result without evidence; treat customer misuse
as the first explanation without listening.

**Choice Architecture — help customers choose by explaining:** category/purpose; primary
approved value; variant/fragrance/flavour where relevant; size or portion; use; important
differences; price and value; support. Too many options without structure increase effort and
wrong selection.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Food-Service Experience Reference ("Mewadi" Analogical Evidence)
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
The canonical Volume IX architecture includes Mewadi food-service and franchise
evidence. Its transferable CX lesson is that product experience includes: menu clarity; product
availability; preparation/presentation consistency; cleanliness and environment; service
behaviour; order accuracy; waiting expectation; price/value understanding; recovery.

**These references do not create unsupported Muv product rules or duplicate Mewadi business
ownership.**

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Menu & Catalogue Experience & Purchase Experience
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Whether menu, product catalogue, website, rate list, or marketplace: use current
products; group logically; provide correct images; state relevant product information; identify
size/quantity; show current price according to channel rules; avoid unavailable or obsolete
items; support comparison.

**Purchase should make:** selection clear; price/offer understandable; quantity accurate;
payment secure and confirmed; terms visible; next steps predictable; help reachable.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Delivery Experience
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Figure 2.2 — Delivery Experience System:** Order confirmation → Preparation →
Quality/accuracy check → Protective packing → Handover → Tracking/communication → Delivery →
Issue route.

**The customer should receive:** correct product and quantity; intact and suitable packaging;
current product; accurate documentation; realistic timing; clear support route.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: First-Use Experience & Usage Education
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
First use often decides whether the customer trusts the product. **Support:**
opening and dispensing; directions and dosage; expected appearance, fragrance, texture, or
presentation where relevant; safety and storage; what result can reasonably be expected; where
to ask questions.

**Usage education should be:** available before and after purchase; consistent across label,
listing, website, sales, and support; specific to product/version; easy to understand; approved;
**free from invented hacks or extended uses.**

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Repeat Purchase & Product Experience Signals
Quality Escalation & Decision Points
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Escalate when feedback suggests:** safety concern; contamination; wrong
product/batch; repeated leakage; abnormal appearance or odour; consistent performance failure;
incorrect label/instructions; recurring delivery damage. Preserve product, order, batch, pack,
image, and customer-use context.

**Decision Points, before changing product information or use guidance:** Is the issue a
misunderstanding or product change? Is the proposed answer supported by current product truth?
Does label/listing/training also require change? Which owner approves?

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Treating the product alone as the product experience. Showing unavailable
menu/catalogue items. Giving inconsistent instructions by channel. Failing to record batch/order
context. Labelling every negative experience "customer preference." Sending retention promotions
before resolving first-use issues.

**Best Practices:** Test the journey using the actual current product. Review choice
architecture with real customer questions. Include first-use guidance in launch readiness.
Connect delivery and product-quality evidence. Monitor repeat by cohort and product. Close the
feedback loop with product and manufacturing.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Product and customer use case aligned.
- [ ] Choice information clear and current.
- [ ] Price, size, product, and availability consistent.
- [ ] Purchase and delivery expectations visible.
- [ ] Order/product accuracy checks operate.
- [ ] First-use guidance approved.
- [ ] Support route easy to find.
- [ ] Product-quality signals linked to batch/order.
- [ ] Repeat and retention reflect real value.
- [ ] Technical issues routed to owning systems.

**Key Takeaways:** The product experience includes selection, purchase, delivery, use, value,
and support. First use is a major trust moment. Food-service and product contexts both require
clarity, consistency, and recovery. Repeat purchase is earned by delivered value, not reminders
alone.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Food-Service Product Experience connects product truth to the customer's
complete practical and sensory reality. It protects correct choice, delivery, first use,
consistency, and repeat."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Outlet Culture & Environment
governs service philosophy, support channels, communication standards, team behaviour, and
physical/digital environments"* — the sourced justification for Chapter 3 following next.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Support Philosophy & Culture before Script
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Support exists to help the customer move from uncertainty or difficulty toward
clarity, safety, resolution, and trust.

**Figure 3.1 — Customer Service System:** Receive → Listen → Identify → Understand → Respond →
Resolve or escalate → Confirm → Record → Learn.

Service quality is not only speed. It includes: accessibility; accuracy; empathy; ownership;
clarity; fairness; continuity; resolution; learning.

**Culture before Script:** A script cannot repair a culture that avoids ownership. Service
culture requires: respect for every customer; calm listening; no blame; truthful limits;
permission to escalate; cross-functional cooperation; accurate records; leadership attention to
repeated friction.

> **Customer Experience Rule** — Never make the customer carry Muv's internal coordination
> problem.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Outlet & Physical Environment
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Where Muv or an associated customer-facing operation uses a physical outlet,
counter, retail point, demonstration area, or partner location, experience includes:
recognition and cleanliness; product/menu organisation; accessibility; staff readiness; waiting
and queue clarity; accurate pricing; product availability; demonstration/use safety; billing;
pickup or delivery handoff; complaint route.

The canonical food-service evidence also highlights environment, menu/product experience,
culture, and service as connected—not separate.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Digital Environment
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Digital customer experience includes: website and marketplace clarity; mobile
usability; product search and selection; accurate content; cart and checkout; payment;
confirmation; tracking; help and accessibility; privacy and security; error recovery.

Technology owns implementation; CX owns the customer outcome and evidence.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Communication Standards & Listening Standard
Query Handling & Support Channels
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Query type | Primary route |
|---|---|
| Product selection | Product-approved guidance |
| Product use | Current directions/FAQ |
| Order/payment | Sales/channel operations |
| Delivery | Fulfilment/distribution |
| Return/refund | Approved channel policy |
| Product quality | Quality/product investigation |
| Safety | Immediate escalation |
| Business/partner | Commercial owner |
| Brand/media | Marketing/brand owner |
| Technical/digital | Platform support owner |

**Support Channels:** phone; WhatsApp; email; website form/chat; marketplace messages; social
messages/comments; retail/outlet; salesperson/partner. **Each requires:** owner; access
control; service hours/expectation; response method; identity verification where needed; record
capture; escalation; continuity.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Response System & Service Response Quality
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
1. Acknowledge. 2. Verify customer/case
context. 3. Classify and prioritise. 4. Provide an approved answer or action. 5. Escalate with
complete context when required. 6. Keep the customer updated. 7. Confirm resolution. 8. Record
outcome and learning.

**Service Response Quality:**

| Dimension | Quality question |
|---|---|
| Correctness | Is the answer supported and current? |
| Completeness | Does it address the real question? |
| Clarity | Can the customer act without reinterpreting? |
| Tone | Is it respectful and human? |
| Ownership | Is a next owner/action visible? |
| Timeliness | Is the response appropriate to urgency and expectation? |
| Resolution | Was the customer outcome completed? |
| Record | Can Muv learn and continue later? |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Escalation Process & Service Documentation
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
safety; legal/compliance risk; product quality; high
financial/reputation impact; vulnerable customer; repeated failure; data/privacy/security;
executive/partner impact; unresolved authority.

**Define:** trigger; destination; information required; immediate containment; update
ownership; resolution authority.

> **WARNING** — Never delay a safety or serious product-quality escalation while attempting to
> satisfy a normal response target.

**Service Documentation — every case record should include:** case ID; customer/contact/
channel; consent/privacy handling where relevant; product/SKU, order, batch if available;
issue/question; dates and interactions; classification/severity; evidence; action and owner;
escalation; resolution; customer confirmation; learning link.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Response Templates, Training & Environment Review
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
acknowledgement; information request; order update;
product-use answer; delay; escalation; resolution; closure; feedback request. Templates must be
adapted to the actual case. Never use empathy language that is contradicted by no action.

**Training — customer-facing teams should learn:** Muv philosophy and brand language; product
truth and use; channel/order systems; support policies; listening; clear writing and speaking;
escalation; complaint and safety handling; documentation; privacy and professionalism; recovery
authority. Assess competence through realistic scenarios.

**Environment Review — from the customer perspective:** Can the customer recognise Muv? Can
they find the right product? Is information correct? Is the next action obvious? Is help
reachable? What happens when a process fails? Are accessibility and dignity protected?

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Measuring service only by first response. Using scripts before
understanding the issue. Asking customers to repeat information. Treating social messages as
non-service. Escalating without context. Closing a case when transferred. Leaving physical/
digital environment problems outside CX ownership.

**Best Practices:** Use one case identity across channels. Maintain an approved knowledge base.
Train for normal and high-risk scenarios. Give teams clear escalation and recovery authority.
Review case quality, not only volume. Observe the actual customer environment.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Support philosophy and ownership clear.
- [ ] Channels have accountable owners.
- [ ] Customer identity/context verified appropriately.
- [ ] Listening and classification complete.
- [ ] Answer uses current approved knowledge.
- [ ] Safety and quality triggers active.
- [ ] Escalation includes full context.
- [ ] Customer updates and next steps clear.
- [ ] Resolution confirmed.
- [ ] Case and learning recorded.
- [ ] Teams trained and assessed.
- [ ] Physical/digital environment reviewed.

**Key Takeaways:** Service combines accuracy, empathy, ownership, and resolution. Culture
determines whether scripts create trust. Every support channel belongs to one connected service
system. Escalation must protect the customer before the metric.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Outlet Culture & Environment turns Muv's customer-first intention into
daily service behaviour across people, places, support channels, and digital experiences."*
Source's own transition line: *"Next: Customer Communication & Promotion governs complaints,
recovery, feedback, reviews, and trust restoration"* — the sourced justification for Chapter 4
following next, and independent confirmation of Chapter 4's already-identified
complaint/recovery-focused real scope.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Complaint Philosophy & Listening before Responding
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
A complaint is: a customer experience requiring response; evidence of possible
failure or expectation mismatch; an opportunity to restore trust; a source of organisational
learning. It is not automatically proof of technical cause. It must be respected and verified.

**Listening before Responding — begin with:** 1. What happened? 2. What did the customer
expect? 3. What was the impact? 4. Which product/order/channel/location was involved? 5. Is
there a safety or urgent risk? 6. What evidence is available? 7. What outcome is the customer
seeking? Do not begin with defence, policy, or blame.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Complaint Classification & Customer Recovery Loop
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Product | Performance, appearance, fragrance, consistency, damage |
| Packaging | Leakage, pump/closure, label, opening, quantity |
| Information | Listing, instructions, price, claim, selection mismatch |
| Order | Wrong, missing, duplicate, cancelled |
| Delivery | Delay, damage, failed delivery, behaviour |
| Service | No response, repeated contact, poor handling |
| Payment/refund | Charge, settlement, delay |
| Safety | Reaction, contamination, dangerous use, incident |
| Preference | Sensory or personal preference without verified failure |

**Figure 4.1 — Customer Recovery Loop:** Listen → Protect → Acknowledge → Investigate →
Resolve → Explain → Confirm → Learn → Prevent recurrence.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Immediate Protection & Root-Cause Understanding
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
advise an appropriate safe stop/use
action through approved guidance; preserve product, pack, order, batch, images, and context;
escalate; identify possibly affected customers/product; avoid unsupported medical, technical,
or legal conclusions.

**Root-Cause Understanding — connect customer evidence with:** approved product specification;
batch/manufacturing record; packaging; listing/marketing claim; order and fulfilment; storage
and transport; use and instructions; previous cases. **Separate:** customer statement; support
observation; technical investigation; verified root cause; final resolution.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Resolution Framework & Service Recovery
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Resolution area | Question |
|---|---|
| Customer need | What fair outcome addresses the present impact? |
| Evidence | What can be established now? |
| Authority | What may the case owner approve? |
| Policy | What current approved terms apply? |
| Risk | Is wider containment or escalation required? |
| Learning | What system may need correction? |

Possible approved outcomes may include information, guidance, replacement, refund, correction,
service action, investigation, or other authorised remedy. This volume does not invent
universal compensation.

**Service Recovery — quality depends on:** prompt acknowledgement; honest ownership;
appropriate apology; practical action; reliable updates; fair resolution; confirmation;
prevention. An apology without action can feel empty. Action without acknowledgement can feel
mechanical.

> **Customer Experience Rule** — Recovery must never require the customer to prove the same
> verified fact repeatedly.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Trust Restoration & Feedback Collection
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
explaining what is known; stating what remains
under investigation; correcting the immediate issue; describing next steps; following through;
preventing repetition; reconnecting later where appropriate. Do not promise that a failure
"will never happen again" without evidence.

**Feedback Collection — collect through:** support cases; reviews; surveys; product-use
follow-up; sales and partner conversations; returns; social listening; community; interviews;
service observation. Each method has bias and limitations.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Review Analysis & Customer Insight
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
product and version; channel/geography; time; rating and text;
verified purchase/context where available; themes; severity; recurrence; response and
resolution; owning function. Do not average away serious safety or quality signals.

**Customer Insight** is stronger than a collection of comments. It connects: Observed pattern +
Customer context + Meaning + Evidence + Business implication. **Before acting:** verify the
pattern; distinguish segment differences; identify root cause; assess affected journey; define
a decision question.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Cross-Functional Learning & Product Improvement Connection
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Feedback theme | Learning owner |
|---|---|
| Product performance/use | Volume V/Product |
| Batch/consistency | Volume VI/Manufacturing & Quality |
| Claim/message | Volume VII/Marketing |
| Price/order/delivery | Volume VIII/Sales & Distribution |
| Pack/design | Volume IV/Design |
| Website/digital | Volume II/Technology ownership |
| Service process | Volume IX/CX |

CX owns the feedback system and follow-through, not every corrective action.

**Product Improvement Connection:** Verified customer evidence may initiate a
product-improvement question, but Volume V owns the product decision and Volume VI owns
manufacturing correction. CX must preserve the customer context, affected product/version,
recurrence, severity, and resulting decision link without rewriting technical conclusions.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Decision from Customer Evidence, Preventing Repeated Failures & Complaint Metrics
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Signal → Classification →
Verification → Pattern/root cause → Owner → Decision → Controlled change → Follow-up
measurement. Do not convert a single request directly into a permanent product, policy, or
brand rule.

**Preventing Repeated Failures may require:** product or manufacturing CAPA; packaging
correction; listing or instruction change; inventory/fulfilment control; training;
knowledge-base update; system automation; clearer ownership; partner action. Verify
effectiveness through later evidence.

**Complaint Metrics — measure:** volume by type and severity; product/order/channel rate;
repeat contact; time to meaningful response; time to resolution; reopened cases; recovery
outcome; root-cause completion; recurrence; customer effort. Numbers require definitions and
context.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Responding before listening. Treating every complaint as customer misuse.
Offering compensation without investigation or learning. Closing after refund while root cause
remains. Using ratings alone as insight. Converting loud feedback into universal policy.
Failing to tell the customer what happens next.

**Best Practices:** Preserve exact customer wording. Use severity and ownership rules. Link
cases to products, orders, batches, and channels. Communicate knowns and unknowns. Review
recurring themes cross-functionally. Verify that prevention worked.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Complaint acknowledged and listened to.
- [ ] Safety/urgency assessed.
- [ ] Exact product/order/channel context captured.
- [ ] Evidence preserved.
- [ ] Customer statement separated from technical conclusion.
- [ ] Resolution authority and next step clear.
- [ ] Customer updated.
- [ ] Resolution confirmed.
- [ ] Root cause and owner recorded where required.
- [ ] Learning routed across functions.
- [ ] Recurrence prevention verified.

**Key Takeaways:** Complaints are customer outcomes and evidence. Recovery begins with
listening and protection. Fair resolution and root-cause prevention are separate obligations.
Feedback becomes a rule only after validation and authority.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Customer Communication & Promotion establishes how Muv listens,
resolves, restores trust, and converts customer evidence into cross-functional improvement
without inventing causes or promises."* Source's own transition line: *"Next: Experience,
Franchise & Expansion References governs loyalty, community, consistency across partners,
metrics, training, and future CX leadership"* — the sourced justification for Chapter 5
following next, confirming Chapter 5 as Part IX's final chapter.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Loyalty Philosophy & Repeat Purchase Thinking
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Loyalty is not repeated purchase created by inconvenience, discount dependency, or
lack of alternatives. It is a continuing preference built through value and trust.

**Figure 5.1 — Relationship Development:** Useful promise → Reliable experience → Fair recovery
→ Repeated value → Emotional trust → Participation → Advocacy.

**Repeat Purchase Thinking — may be influenced by:** product performance; availability; value;
correct use; convenience; habit; service; trust; replenishment timing; relevant communication.
Analyse repeat by product, channel, cohort, and customer context. Do not interpret all
non-repeat as rejection without evidence.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Retention & Loyalty Principles
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
support successful use; make replenishment
easy; maintain availability; remember relevant preferences with appropriate permission; respond
to problems; communicate useful information; avoid excessive pressure. Retention belongs to the
complete experience, not only marketing automation.

**Loyalty Principles:** 1. Earn before asking. 2. Deliver consistent value. 3. Recognise
without intruding. 4. Reward without confusing economics or fairness. 5. Make benefits
understandable. 6. Preserve customer choice. 7. Learn from both repeat and departure.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Emotional Connection & Community Building
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
recognition;
confidence; respect; shared values; useful progress; reliable care; belonging. It cannot be
scripted into existence while product and service remain inconsistent.

**Community Building — a Muv community should provide mutual value through:** useful product
education; routines and problem-solving; questions and feedback; local participation; shared
Keep Muving™ meaning; early learning; responsible customer stories with permission.

> **WARNING** — Do not label a broadcast list a community or use community access to bypass
> customer communication preferences.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Advocacy
Franchise & Partner Experience & Partner Experience Standards
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Customers should encounter the same central promise across company, outlet,
franchise, distributor, retailer, marketplace, and service partner.

**Figure 5.2 — Experience Governance across Partners:** Central promise and standards → Partner
selection → Onboarding → Training → Local execution → Measurement → Recovery → Improvement.

The franchise business model belongs to Volume X. This chapter owns customer-facing
consistency: product/menu information; service behaviour; environment; pricing clarity;
availability; complaint routes; handoffs; experience records.

**Partner Experience Standards — every customer-facing partner should know:** what Muv
promises; current product and information; approved service behaviour; what may and may not be
promised; how to handle and record questions; when and how to escalate; how customer evidence
returns to Muv.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Expansion & Experience & Expansion Readiness Gate
Experience Measurement, CX Metrics & Measurement Discipline
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Promise → Journey measure →
Operational evidence → Customer perception → Outcome → Learning.

| Layer | Examples |
|---|---|
| Accessibility | Can customers find information and support? |
| Effort | How difficult is selection, purchase, use, or resolution? |
| Reliability | Order accuracy, delivery, product consistency, response completion |
| Perception | Satisfaction, trust, clarity, confidence |
| Behaviour | Repeat, retention, advocacy, churn |
| Recovery | Resolution, repeat contact, reopened cases, recurrence |
| Learning | Root causes, actions, effectiveness |

**CX Metrics — potential metrics require defined methods:** satisfaction after a specific
interaction; customer effort; recommendation/advocacy measure; repeat or retention;
first-contact or end-to-end resolution; complaint and severity rate; response and resolution
time; contact rate by journey; review themes; trust/clarity research. No metric alone defines
experience quality.

**Measurement Discipline — for each metric define:** question; scope; customer; event/timing;
method; sample; calculation; owner; limitation; decision use. Do not compare numbers collected
through materially different methods as if they were identical.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: CX Ownership & Experience Decision Record
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Rhythm | Review |
|---|---|
| Daily | High-risk cases, service queue, active incidents |
| Weekly | Friction, backlog, escalations, repeated questions |
| Monthly | Journey metrics, complaint patterns, recovery, cross-functional actions |
| Launch/market review | Readiness, first-use questions, fulfilment, returns, feedback |
| Quarterly | Trust, retention, partner consistency, capability |
| Annual | Experience strategy, standards, systems, culture, future needs |

**Figure 5.4 — Customer Experience Decision Record:**

| Field | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Decision ID | Stable identifier |
| Journey/customer scope | Exact affected experience |
| Evidence | Customer voice, operational data, root cause, risk |
| Alternatives | Options considered |
| Authority/date | Who decided and when |
| Status | Approved, partially approved, rejected, deferred, research required, open, or superseded |
| Decision/rationale | What changes and why |
| Owners | Responsible functions |
| Standards/systems affected | Journey, policy, product, service, training, partner |
| Validation | How improvement will be verified |

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Training, Knowledge Transfer & Continuous Improvement Culture
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Muv philosophy and promise; journey
awareness; current product/channel knowledge; communication and listening; service and
escalation; complaints and recovery; documentation; privacy and dignity; cross-functional
ownership. Use scenarios drawn from validated case types without inventing customer stories.

**Knowledge Transfer should preserve:** journey maps and standards; current knowledge base;
case categories; escalation matrix; open high-risk cases; recurring themes; decisions and
improvement actions; partner/outlet differences; metric definitions; customer research
limitations.

**Figure 5.5 — Customer Experience Improvement Cycle:** Observe → Listen → Measure → Verify →
Prioritise → Decide → Change → Train → Re-measure → Preserve learning.

Improvement should prioritise: safety and trust; severe failures; high-frequency friction;
unnecessary customer effort; broken handoffs; expectation mismatch; repeated partner variation.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Future CX Leadership & Decision Points
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
customer dignity; truth; cross-functional
accountability; visible failure; fair recovery; learning; long-term trust. **They should ask:**
What promise did the customer hear? What reality did they receive? Where did Muv make them work
unnecessarily? What failure repeats? What evidence is missing? Has recovery restored trust?
What must change across the company?

**Decision Points — do not scale loyalty, community, franchise, partner, or market programmes
until:** the core experience is reliable; governance and support are ready; customer
communication preferences are protected; metrics and escalation operate; local learning is
available.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Chapter Governance Summary
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
**Common Mistakes:** Equating repeat purchase with loyalty. Using discounts as the complete
retention strategy. Creating a community with no member value. Expanding partners without
experience training. Measuring only satisfaction averages. Leaving CX knowledge inside one
leader. Launching improvements without remeasurement.

**Best Practices:** Earn advocacy through reliable value. Segment repeat and churn evidence.
Give communities clear purpose and choice. Certify partner readiness before customer
activation. Use operational and perception metrics together. Maintain decision and learning
history. Train future leaders across the full journey.

**Action Checklist:**
- [ ] Repeat and loyalty distinguished.
- [ ] Retention supports real product success.
- [ ] Community has mutual value and permission.
- [ ] Advocacy is authentic.
- [ ] Partner/franchise experience standards defined.
- [ ] Expansion readiness includes support and recovery.
- [ ] Metrics have controlled definitions.
- [ ] CX governance has owners and rhythms.
- [ ] Decisions link customer and operational evidence.
- [ ] Training and knowledge transfer complete.
- [ ] Improvement is remeasured.
- [ ] Future leadership can trace experience evolution.

**Key Takeaways:** Loyalty is earned through repeated value and trust. Community and advocacy
must remain voluntary and authentic. Expansion requires experience readiness across every
partner. CX governance connects measurement, ownership, training, decisions, and continuous
improvement.

**Chapter Summary:** *"Experience, Franchise & Expansion References establishes the long-term
relationship and governance layer of Muv customer experience. It protects loyalty, community,
partner consistency, measurement, and future leadership."* Source's own transition line:
*"Next: Volume X continues the Knowledge Library with MUV Business Blueprint™—the architecture
governing business model, expansion, franchise, legal, compliance, and company systems."*

**Part End Note (Part IX's own closing note, verbatim):** *"Volume IX establishes MUV Customer
Experience™ as the official operating system for customer journeys, product and service
experience, complaints, recovery, feedback, loyalty, community, partner consistency,
measurement, and experience governance. Muv earns long-term trust when every promise is matched
by reality, every customer is treated with dignity, every problem receives ownership, and every
interaction strengthens the company's ability to serve better next time. Volume X continues the
MUV Knowledge Library™ with MUV Business Blueprint™."* Part X is out of scope for this domain
and is cited here only for completeness, not transcribed.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Part IX Summary: MUV Customer Experience in One View
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
| Experience area | Permanent standard |
|---|---|
| Philosophy | Customer experience is the company-wide result of promise and interaction |
| Trust | Tell the truth, deliver consistently, respect the customer, recover fairly |
| Journey | Design from awareness through advocacy |
| Product experience | Connect choice, delivery, use, value, and support |
| Service | Listen, understand, own, resolve, record, and learn |
| Handoffs | Transfer context and ownership without transferring customer effort |
| Complaints | Protect, investigate, resolve, restore, and prevent |
| Feedback | Validate signals before creating permanent rules |
| Loyalty | Earn continuing preference through real value |
| Community | Provide mutual value with choice and authenticity |
| Partners | Extend one promise through training and governance |
| Measurement | Combine operational evidence, customer perception, and behaviour |
| Leadership | Protect dignity, truth, accountability, and continuous learning |

**Master Customer Experience Principles:** 1. Experience is the complete reality of the
promise. 2. Listen before responding. 3. Protect customer dignity and safety. 4. Make ownership
visible. 5. Do not make customers navigate internal structure. 6. Resolve the present issue and
prevent repetition. 7. Separate customer evidence from assumed cause. 8. Earn loyalty before
asking for it. 9. Measure the journey, not one score. 10. Preserve learning across the company.

**Master Customer Experience Checklist:**
- [ ] Promise and customer reality aligned.
- [ ] Journey stages, touchpoints, and moments of truth mapped.
- [ ] Owners and handoffs explicit.
- [ ] Product, purchase, delivery, first-use, and repeat experiences controlled.
- [ ] Support channels connected.
- [ ] Communication uses current approved information.
- [ ] Complaint and safety escalation operating.
- [ ] Recovery authority and records clear.
- [ ] Feedback linked to product, manufacturing, marketing, sales, and technology.
- [ ] Loyalty, community, and advocacy remain authentic.
- [ ] Partner and expansion readiness verified.
- [ ] Metrics defined and balanced.
- [ ] CX decisions and improvement effectiveness recorded.
- [ ] Training and knowledge transfer complete.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: CRM as Commercial Memory & the Fourteen Maintained Fields
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
CRM is the commercial memory of relationships and commitments.

**Maintain:** account/contact identity; role and consent/preference; source; need and
qualification; territory/channel; interactions; opportunity stage/value; products and terms;
objections; samples/proposals; next action; orders, fulfilment, collection; complaint/service
links; owner and history.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: CRM Data Quality Discipline
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
CRM quality must not be judged by field completion alone. Data must support
decisions and handovers.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Business Intelligence Discipline
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Business intelligence should connect measures to decisions.

**A useful intelligence product states:** the question; the definition of each measure; the
period and scope; the source; known limitations; comparison or context; responsible owner; and
the decision or action it informs.

Dashboards that accumulate numbers without decisions create visibility theatre.

knowledgeItemProjections.title: Customer Insights: Evidence Sources & the Observation-vs-Explanation Rule
knowledgeItemProjections.content:
Customer insight may combine: purchase and journey evidence; search and content
behaviour; support interactions; reviews and feedback; returns and complaints; research;
channel patterns; and product-use learning where appropriately obtained.

Observation is not explanation. Muv must distinguish what happened from why it happened.
